newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Duma, govt go for brinkmanship in Russian budget.
newsitem.headline: Duma, govt go for brinkmanship in Russian budget.

text.p: The battle for Russia's 1997 budget has turned into a game of brinkmanship between communist deputies determined to squeeze out as many concessions as possible and a government anxious to keep reforms on track.

Analysts say Russia's credibility as a reforming nation is at stake, together, perhaps, with Moscow's ability to receive injections of cash from the International Monetary Fund next year as part of a three-year loan programme.

"They need credibility on macro-economic targets for the IMF programme and it makes it harder to establish credibility without a budget," said Charles Blitzer, chief economist, emerging markets, at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
"But if the budget is inconsistent with the three-year programme, that also raises a problem."
The 1996 budget already faces problems and the State Duma lower house of parliament, dominated by communists and their conservative allies, has rejected a draft 1997 budget once.
Deputies are due to discuss an amended plan on Wednesday or on Friday.
Many deputies, accusing the government of doing too little to protect Russians who have lost out in free-market economic reforms, have promised not to give up without a fight.
Gennady Kulik, a conservative agrarian who is deputy chairman of the Duma's budget committee said on Monday that it would "take a miracle" to approve the latest plan.

He said farms needed loans and said the central bank should issue credits to help fund the budget deficit, targeted at 3.5 percent of gross domestic product in the latest draft. The gap has already been widened from 3.3 percent in the first proposal.
Most ministers have vowed not to print money, fearing it could unleash inflation as the economy is starting to stabilise. But some say Russia may not need the IMF cash.

"The advice of the IMF on Russian economic reform is solely in the nature of a recommendation from Moscow's point of view," Foreign Trade Minister Oleg Davydov was quoted as saying on Monday. "We listen to it but take the decisions ourselves."
Christopher Granville, chief economist at United City Bank, said Russia could end the year without a 1997 budget.

"Parliament does not want to let this budget through, but on the other hand they do not want a confrontation," he said. "It could get to the funny situation where you are trundling along next year without a budget."
Russia, still struggling to reverse years of painful economic decline, has managed without budgets before, fixing spending by decree based on what took place the previous year.
But conservative deputies eventually backed down each year and approved the spending plans.

"We have seen brinkmanship in the past, but things are slightly different this year," said one economist. "Inflation is lower and there are no elections, which means you cannot offer deputies money for campaigning and hope to get their vote."
But he still expected a budget to be approved before the end of this year. "It is in everybody's interests."
Finance Minsister Alexander Livshits said last week a 1997 budget was not a precondition for the $10 billion IMF loan.
But he added: "It's quite obvious that any country which respects itself has to have a budget before the beginning of the budget year."
Problems with the 1996 budget centre on tax income, which is well below plan. The IMF delayed paying one tranche of the loan last month and told Russia to do more to make tax debtors pay.
If the Duma does not approve this week's first reading of the budget, the government has 20 days to draw up new proposals.

The next stage could be a vote of confidence in the government, and a no-confidence vote would force President Boris Yeltsin to choose whether to dismiss the government or dissolve parliament and call new elections.
Yeltsin is currently recovering from open heart surgery, but aides say he will be back in the Kremlin early next year.
"It is a particularly dangerous game at a time when Yeltsin is coming back to work," said Blitzer.
